title: A linear model trained on noisy labels still knows which labels are wrong: out-of-fold disagreement as a noise filter
insight: Even when 40% of the labels are flipped, a logistic regression's out-of-fold disagreements with its training labels are mostly the flipped ones, so dropping them and refitting wins back much of the lost accuracy with no clean validation set and no noise-rate estimate.
abstract_sketch: Label noise lowers the accuracy of simple classifiers, and the usual fixes need a clean validation set or an estimate of the noise rate. We observe that a logistic regression fit on noisy labels still disagrees mostly with the labels that are wrong: when we predict each training sample from a model that never saw it, most of the disagreements are flipped labels, and most flipped labels are among them. We turn this observation into a filter: fit with 5-fold cross-validation, drop every sample whose out-of-fold prediction disagrees with its label, and refit on the rest. On two small scikit-learn datasets with symmetric noise up to 40%, the filter wins back most of the accuracy noise costs on digits, beats a logistic regression trained on the noisy labels, beats an untuned MLP by a wide margin, and costs little on clean labels. It recovers less on breast cancer at 40% noise, it throws away some clean samples, and we do not compare it with co-teaching or confident learning.
figure1: Three panels on one shared noise axis (0, 20, 40% symmetric label noise). Panel (a), the observation: a small cartoon of a training set with flipped labels in red, 5-fold out-of-fold predictions as arrows, and the samples where the arrow disagrees with the label circled; beside it a grouped bar chart (digits and breast cancer, 20% and 40% noise) of the share of circled samples that are truly flipped (precision) and the share of flipped labels that are circled (recall), with seed points and sd error bars. Panel (b), the fix: a three-step diagram (fit out-of-fold, drop disagreements, refit) in the accent purple. Panel (c), the result: test accuracy against noise rate for digits and breast cancer, with the filter in purple, logistic regression on noisy labels, and the MLP each in a fixed muted color, and the clean-label logistic regression as a gray dashed reference line; error bars are sd over 5 seeds. The panels together show that the disagreement signal is informative and that using it closes much of the gap.
contributions: We show that a logistic regression trained on noisy labels flags mostly the flipped labels through its out-of-fold disagreements, at 20% and 40% symmetric noise on two datasets.

We propose an out-of-fold filter that drops these samples and refits, which needs no clean validation set and no noise-rate estimate, and show that it recovers most of the accuracy lost to noise on digits and beats an untuned MLP trained on the same noisy labels in every seed.

We measure what the filter costs: it changes accuracy on clean labels by less than a quarter of a point, discards correct samples (a quarter to a third of its drops under noise), and recovers only about a fifth of the lost accuracy on breast cancer at 40% noise.
storyline: Label noise hurts even simple linear classifiers, and common remedies need a clean validation set or a noise-rate estimate that practitioners rarely have. The observation is that the damage does not erase the model's knowledge: a logistic regression fit on noisy labels, asked to predict each training sample from folds that exclude it, disagrees with the given label mostly when the label is wrong. Out-of-fold prediction is what makes this work, because a model cannot memorize the label of a sample it has not seen, and the flipped labels are scattered rather than systematic, so the clean majority outvotes them. The filter follows directly: drop the disagreements and refit. On digits and breast cancer the dropped samples are mostly flipped, the refit model beats the unfiltered one under noise, and it beats an untuned MLP, which degrades faster, by a large margin in every seed. The signal weakens as the noise rate grows, so the filter recovers most of the lost accuracy on digits but only part of it on breast cancer at 40% noise, and it never returns to clean-label accuracy at 40%. What this changes is a cheap, assumption-light baseline for noisy-label work on linear models, and a reason to look at out-of-fold disagreement before reaching for heavier machinery.

risks: First attack: two small datasets, symmetric noise only, five seeds. We state the scope in the setup and limitations, report paired tests and intervals, and make no claim about deep networks or large data. Second: the MLP is untuned, so the margin may reflect the baseline; we say it is one untuned MLP, report that the MLP wins slightly on clean digits, and keep the claim to 'beats this MLP under noise'. Third: no comparison with co-teaching or confident learning; we cite them and state that we cannot claim to outperform them. Fourth: 'most' fails on breast cancer at 40% noise and the breast cancer gain at 20% is not significant; we report both as limits and tie the weaker recovery to the weaker disagreement signal at high noise rather than hide it. Fifth: the filter discards correct samples; we report the clean-drop share and its small accuracy cost. Timing is a single unrecorded-machine measurement, so it is mentioned only with that limit.
